Share it with your friends! Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn Romania's Senate on August 5 approved the Integrity Law, a key milestone under the country's National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR), sending the legislation to President Nicușor Dan for promulgation, according to Curs de Guvernare . The bill includes two controversial amendments backed by the Social Democratic Party (PSD) and the far-right Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR), which critics argue risk being struck down by the Constitutional Court. The law was adopted by 104 votes to eight, with seven abstentions and two senators not voting. One AUR senator, six Save Romania Union (USR) senators and one unaffiliated senator voted against the bill. According to Curs de Guvernare, the legislation could jeopardize a EUR 790 million grant under the European Union's Recovery and Resilience Facility if it is declared unconstitutional. The president may return the law to Parliament for reconsideration once before deciding whether to promulgate it. One of the disputed amendments, promoted primarily by PSD, would bar from holding public office dignitaries who had previously been found to be in a conflict of interest. The provision is widely seen as targeting Timișoara Mayor Dominic Fritz, who also serves as president of the opposition USR. A second amendment, proposed by AUR, extends asset declaration requirements to spouses and "spouse-like partners" of public officials. Legal experts, including former Constitutional Court judges cited by Curs de Guvernare, have criticized the wording as too vague to meet constitutional standards. President Dan's partner, Mirabela Grădinaru, published her declarations of assets and interests on August 5. On August 3, USR accused PSD and AUR of negotiating amendments designed to target political opponents. "At the behest of Sorin Grindeanu, PSD and AUR insist on creating retroactive punishments to eliminate their opponents from office, even if this means democratic vandalism and pushing Romania towards illiberalism," USR said in a statement. The party warned that Romania could lose "almost EUR 800 million" in European funding if the legislation is ultimately found to breach constitutional principles. https://www.politico.eu/article/eurocrat.text: BRUSSELS — Most EU countries support slashing the bloc’s personnel costs to make savings as part of the next long-term budget , the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU wrote in a document seen by POLITICO. The EU’s 27 governments are clashing over the size of the common cashpot, with a group of countries led by Germany calling for several hundred billion euros of cuts to a Commission proposal for a €2 trillion Multiannual Financial Framework for 2028-2034. But a rival camp of countries that includes Italy and Poland supports more spending on agriculture and poorer regions. Despite such disagreements, the running costs of the EU institutions — such as officials’ salaries and building expenses — have emerged as the most likely budget item to face cuts. Advertisement Advertisement The Irish presidency, which is steering the budget talks, wrote that “reductions could be made, with many [countries] questioning the justification of the proposed increase in staff levels” at a time when they’re making domestic personnel cuts. The Commission proposed hiring an extra 2,500 officials over the next seven years, fueling discontent from nine countries led by Austria. In the Commission's proposal, which was drawn up in July 2025, administrative costs will be worth €118 billion from 2028 to 2034, which is around 6% of the overall budget. However, Ireland is facing strong resistance to cutting other areas of the budget. The Irish presidency wrote in the document that most capitals oppose reductions in agricultural spending and regional payouts, which it described as countries' “most important priority.” Ireland hinted that the overall budget might face cuts as countries opposed increasing their national contributions and challenged new EU-wide taxes to finance the budget. “These factors point to a need to reflect on our level of ambition for expenditure increases,” the Irish wrote. During a meeting on Wednesday, Dublin will sound out the EU’s 27 ambassadors on which budget items they want to downsize. "Are there any other elements in terms of changes to the Negotiating Box [the working document that guides budget talks] that would be helpful in formulating your views regarding the expenditure level?" it wrote. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/17/nort.text: North Korea said on Saturday that it had tested a new AI-powered torpedo system as it continues a wave of recent weapons demonstrations.The country's KCNA state news agency reported that the test involved the "super-speed, precisely guided" Zam-2.0 torpedo system, which it said uses artificial intelligence to aid with target detection and guidance.The report said the test had verified the weapon's propulsion systems.It comes after North Korea also tested two types of underwater-launched strategic cruise missiles on Wednesday as part of what is believed to be a push to bolster its naval capabilities. The missiles are thought to have been fired from a submarine.North Korea has also carried out a number of ballistic missile tests in recent weeks as it seeks to build up its arsenal amid growing tensions with neighbouring South Korea.In August, US President Donald Trump told reporters that North Korean leader Kim Jong-un had "57 very powerful nuclear weapons" as he once again touted the pair's relationship."You know what, the fact that I get along with him, that's a good thing not a bad thing," Trump said, adding that Pyongyang's nuclear arsenal should "never" have been allowed to happen.Trump said at the time that he intended to meet with Kim later this year, although he gave no further details on the plan.The president also claimed earlier this month that he was preventing a war between North and South Korea "on a constant basis."

https://tribune.com.pk/story/2633028/pro.text: Home World Pro-Europe Latvian PM wins Russia-dominated poll . Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs' centre-right party emerged as the victor on Sunday from Latvia's parliamentary election, and he will now set about forming a coalition to maintain his pro-European and pro-Ukrainian course. Populist parties, boosted by support from Latvia's Russian-speaking minority, also had a good night after an election campaign dominated by fears over neighbouring Russia, the cost of living and other social issues. Kulbergs' United List party won 42 seats in the 100-seat parliament -- an unprecedented result in the former Soviet republic's post-independence history. After exit polls hinted at the magnitude of his party's victory, Kulbergs said it was a wider margin than he had expected. "That means people truly want change," he said, which he said meant "economic growth" and a future for the country's children. Kulbergs, a former manager in the telecoms and automotive sectors, took over as prime minister in May at the head of a centre-right coalition. He will be forced to change partners after the election, as one of his members failed to clear the five-percent hurdle to get into parliament. 'Strong border' Security remains central to political debate in Latvia, more than four years after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Latvia, a member of NATO and the European Union since 2004, views Russia as its principal security threat and has significantly increased defence spending in response. "Because we are the external border of Europe, we must have a strong economy... a strong border region," Kulbergs said. "That is the main task." But rising living costs, low wages, strains on the healthcare system and long-term population decline all featured prominently in campaign debates. While most parties expected to enter parliament back both high military spending and maintaining aid to Kyiv, the right-wing Sovereign Power party has broken ranks. It has opposed military aid to Ukraine and further increases to defence spending. It looked set for a third-place finish, with 15 MPs, after focusing on cost of living issues. Right-wing populist parties Soverign Power has been tarred pro-Russian by its detractors and most major parties have ruled out working with it. Latvia First, a conservative party run by a property magnate often compared toh US President Donald Trump, came second in the poll and took 17 seats. Both populist parties benefitted from changes in voting patterns among the Russian-speaking minority, who make up a third of the population. They had long rallied around Harmony, which was at one time the country's biggest party. But Harmony was broadly seen as pro-Kremlin and its support collapsed dramatically in the last election, held shortly after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
